name: MLX
title: How MLX Runs on Apple Silicon: Lazy Graphs, Metal | Language Lineage
h1: What Actually Happens When You Run MLX on a Mac?
description: Trace MLX code on Apple silicon: lazy compute graph, eval(), Metal GPU kernels or C++ CPU kernels, and what mx.compile fuses, in unified memory, with sources.
og_subtitle: Python → lazy graph → eval() → Metal kernels · C++ CPU kernels → Apple silicon
verified_against: the MLX documentation (Lazy Evaluation, Unified Memory, Compilation, Custom Extensions, Build and Install), the MLX README, and the Metal and CPU compile sources in ml-explore/mlx
scope: Documented paths for MLX Python code on one Apple silicon Mac, run lazily or with mx.compile, on the GPU or the CPU. MLX's CUDA backend for Linux, distributed training, custom Metal kernels written with mx.fast.metal_kernel, and the C++, C and Swift APIs are out of scope.
answer: MLX operations do not compute anything when you call them: they record a **lazy compute graph**. Work happens when the graph is **evaluated**, either by calling **eval()** or implicitly, for example by printing an array. Evaluation runs each operation's primitive on the device you chose: **Metal** kernels on the Apple silicon GPU, or C++ kernels on the CPU. Arrays live in **unified memory**, so both devices use the same data without copies. With **mx.compile**, MLX traces the function once, merges and fuses operations, and generates code: a Metal kernel for the GPU, or a C++ shared library for the CPU.

sections.heading: Lazy by default
paragraphs: Calling **mx.add** or a layer of an **mlx.nn** model only adds a node to a graph. The graph runs when something needs the values: an explicit **mx.eval**, printing an array, converting it to NumPy, or calling **.item()**. A training loop typically evaluates once per step, so each step's forward pass, gradients and optimizer update run as one graph.

That is the main difference from [PyTorch in eager mode](/ai/how-pytorch-runs) and from [JAX without jit](/ai/how-jax-runs), where each operation is dispatched as Python reaches it. **mx.compile** plays the role that torch.compile and jax.jit play there.

sections.heading: One memory, two devices
paragraphs: On Apple silicon the CPU and GPU share one memory pool. MLX arrays do not belong to a device; you pick the device per operation (the **stream** argument), and MLX inserts the dependencies when an operation on one device needs the result of another. That is why the device choice above changes only the kernels, not where the data lives.
For running LLMs locally on a Mac with hand-written Metal kernels instead, compare [how llama.cpp runs a model](/ai/how-llama-cpp-runs).

stages.name: Your MLX code
stages.summary: Python code using mlx.core arrays, and often mlx.nn models and mlx.optimizers.

evidence.quote: MLX has a Python API that closely follows NumPy.

stages.name: MLX
stages.summary: Apple's array framework. Its operations are thin front ends that add nodes to a graph.

evidence.quote: MLX is an array framework for machine learning on Apple silicon, brought to you by Apple machine learning research.
Operations in MLX build the computation graph. Primitives provide the rules for evaluating and transforming the graph.

stages.name: Lazy compute graph
stages.summary: The recorded operations, each a primitive with its inputs. Nothing has been computed yet.

evidence.quote: When you perform operations in MLX, no computation actually happens. Instead a compute graph is recorded.

stages.name: mx.compile
stages.summary: MLX's compiler transformation. On the first call it traces the function with placeholder inputs, shrinks the graph and fuses operations; later calls with the same shapes and types reuse the result.

evidence.quote: Function compilation results in smaller graphs by merging common work and fusing certain operations.
The first time you call a compiled function, MLX will build the compute graph, optimize it, and generate and compile code.

stages.name: Evaluation (eval)
stages.summary: When values are needed, MLX schedules the graph and runs each primitive on the device of its stream.

evidence.quote: The actual computation only happens if an eval() is performed.
When we evaluate the output array, MLX schedules the execution of the computation graph, and calls Axpby::eval_cpu() or Axpby::eval_gpu() depending on the stream/device specified by the user.

stages.name: C++ CPU kernels
stages.summary: Each primitive's CPU implementation (eval_cpu), written in C++.

evidence.quote: A Primitive has methods to run on the CPU or GPU and for function transformations such as vjp and jvp.

stages.name: Fused C++ library
stages.summary: For the CPU, mx.compile generates C++ source for the fused operations, builds it into a shared library and loads it.

evidence.quote: Could not load C++ shared library
The first time you call a compiled function, MLX will build the compute graph, optimize it, and generate and compile code.

stages.name: Metal kernels
stages.summary: Each primitive's GPU implementation (eval_gpu), a kernel written in the Metal shading language and shipped prebuilt in MLX's Metal library.

evidence.quote: Apple silicon devices address their GPUs using the Metal shading language, and GPU kernels in MLX are written using Metal.
the MLX Metal library which contains pre-built GPU kernels

stages.name: Fused Metal kernel
stages.summary: For the GPU, mx.compile writes Metal source for the fused operations and compiles it into one kernel.

stages.name: Apple silicon CPU
stages.summary: The CPU cores, sharing one memory pool with the GPU.

evidence.quote: Apple silicon has a unified memory architecture. The CPU and GPU have direct access to the same memory pool.

stages.name: Apple silicon GPU
